summary: Defines TLS handshake extensions for exchanging authorization data, such as attribute certificates or SAML assertions, once both sides say they support it. The data goes in a supplemental data handshake message. It is an experimental specification.

eli5.summary: Besides showing ID when connecting, you also show a permission slip, if both sides know how to handle one.

questions: how to send saml assertion in tls
what is supplemental data in tls
subtitle: How a TLS client and server can swap authorization data, such as attribute certificates or SAML assertions, during the handshake.

tldr.problem: TLS authenticates the parties, but some environments also need the client or server to present authorization information before any protected data is exchanged.
tldr.mechanism: Two hello extensions, client_authz and server_authz, confirm which authorization formats both sides support, and the data itself then travels in the supplemental data handshake message.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5878 is an Experimental specification that updates RFC 5246 and has since been updated by RFC 8447 and RFC 8996.

today: RFC 5878 is an Experimental specification that updates RFC 5246, and it has been updated by RFC 8447 and RFC 8996. It was published for examination and evaluation rather than as a standard.

sections.title: Why Authorization in the Handshake
sections.content:
TLS is used in more and more environments, including some its designers did not foresee. This RFC adds a way to exchange authorization information between client and server before any protected data flows. It is especially attractive when more than one application protocol can use the same authorization information.

The format of the authorization data is extensible. The RFC defines X.509 attribute certificates and SAML assertions, but says other formats can be used, and that future ones may include any opaque assertion digitally signed by a trusted issuer. It works with TLS 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2.

The RFC is also candid about when not to use it. If each application needs its own authorization information, that information might best be carried inside the TLS-protected application protocol. Care is needed to keep identification, authentication and authorization properly bound when they are handled at different protocol layers.
sections.eli5: Showing your ID tells people who you are. A permission slip tells them what you are allowed to do. This document lets you show the slip at the door, at the same time as your ID.

sections.title: The Two Hello Extensions
sections.content:
Two new extension types are added to the client and server hello messages: client_authz (value 7) and server_authz (value 8). The client includes client_authz to say it wants to send authorization data to the server, and server_authz to say it wants to receive authorization data from the server. Each carries a list of acceptable data formats.

A server that is willing to take part answers with the same extension, with any unacceptable formats removed from the list. If the server cannot accept any of the formats, it MUST omit the extension. This keeps things backwards compatible: authorization data is only sent in a format that both sides announced.

Servers must accept extended client hello messages even if they do not understand every extension, but they will not echo the ones they do not understand. A client may then reject servers that do not support the authorization extensions.

On session resumption, the client SHOULD still include the extensions, in case the resumption request is denied and a full handshake follows. A successful resumption MUST use the same authorization information as the original session.
sections.eli5: The client says "I can show these kinds of permission slips, and I would like to see these kinds from you." The server answers with the kinds it can actually handle. If there is no match, nobody sends slips.

sections.title: Authorization Data Formats and Where They Go
sections.content:
Four formats are defined in the AuthzDataFormat list: x509_attr_cert (0), saml_assertion (1), x509_attr_cert_url (2) and saml_assertion_url (3). The first two carry the data itself. The two URL forms carry a URL plus a one-way hash, because attribute certificates and SAML assertions can be large.

The data travels in the SupplementalData handshake message, using a new supplemental data type authz_data (16386). The server's message comes after its ServerHello and the client's comes before its Certificate. The client SHOULD follow least privilege and send only the authorizations the server is expected to need. This mechanism does not support a back-and-forth where the server answers with new authorization information; such translation services should happen in application data, not in the handshake.

An attribute certificate (AC) is like a public key certificate but contains no public key. It can state group membership, role or security clearance. Its holder field MUST use either baseCertificateID or entityName so it links to the certificate sent in the TLS Certificate message. A SAML assertion MUST be well-formed XML in UTF-8 or UTF-16, with UTF-8 preferred.

For the URL forms, implementations MUST support the http scheme and MUST check that the fetched object matches the hash. They MUST support SHA-1 and SHA-256. The hash is protected by the TLS Finished message. To avoid circular dependencies, a client using HTTP MUST NOT use these extensions if UPGRADE in HTTP is used.
sections.eli5: A permission slip can be handed over directly, or you can give the address of where to fetch it plus a fingerprint to prove it is the right one. The slip goes in a special envelope inside the greeting.

sections.title: Reusing TLS Alerts for Authorization Errors
sections.content:
RFC 5878 does not invent new alerts for authorization failures. It reuses the TLS alerts for certificate processing, and all alerts used in authorization processing are fatal. For example, bad_certificate means an authorization was corrupt or its signature did not verify, certificate_expired means it has expired or is not currently valid, unknown_ca means the issuer is not known and trusted, and access_denied means the authorization was not sufficient to grant access.

Two alerts matter for the URL formats. bad_certificate_hash_value means a downloaded authorization does not match its hash, and certificate_unobtainable means a URL did not yield an authorization. Implementations MUST deny access in the second case.

The RFC warns that alerts are imprecise: the alert does not say which certificate or which authorization caused the error, so implementers should be aware of that.
sections.eli5: If the permission slip is fake, expired or missing, the connection is stopped using the same error messages already used for bad ID cards.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned the extension types client_authz (7) and server_authz (8) from the TLS Extension Type registry, and the supplemental data type authz_data (16386) from the TLS Supplemental Data Type registry.

The RFC also creates a new registry for TLS Authorization Data Formats, with the four formats above as its first entries. Values 0 to 63 are assigned by IETF Review, 64 to 223 by Specification Required, and 224 to 255 are reserved for Private Use.
sections.eli5: The numbers for the new features were officially written down in the Internet's phone book, and a new list was started so more kinds of permission slips can be added later.

sections.title: Security Considerations and the Double Handshake
sections.content:
A TLS server can support several applications, each needing different authorization. A client may supply enough for some but not all. The handshake will still complete, so the server must itself make sure the client can only use the applications and features for which authorization was confirmed.

The SupplementalData message is sent in the unencrypted part of the handshake, and the server's comes before the client is authenticated. A bearer SAML assertion could therefore be captured by an eavesdropper and replayed. Constraints such as short lifetimes, source address limits, destination limits and replay caches help against an eavesdropper but are less likely to help against a man-in-the-middle.

When authorization information is sensitive, the RFC describes a double handshake: a first handshake with no authorization extensions sets up protected communication, then a second handshake that includes the authorization data runs inside it. This ensures both parties are authenticated before either provides authorization information, and it prevents disclosure of a bearer SAML assertion to anyone but the TLS peer. For URL formats, implementations SHOULD adopt a policy of least privilege about which references they will fetch.
sections.eli5: The first greeting is said in the open, so anyone could overhear a permission slip. For secret slips, the two sides first set up a private room, then do a second greeting inside it.

messages.label: ClientHello (w/ extensions)
messages.note: Lists the client_authz and server_authz formats it supports.

messages.label: ServerHello (w/ extensions)
messages.note: Echoes only the formats the server supports.

items.desc: A SAML assertion sent in the handshake.

items.desc: A URL and hash from which to fetch the attribute certificate.
